title: Ending the workday
hookLine: a clear end protects the rest of life

cards: The laptop is closed, but the work isn't. It comes along to dinner, rides home in a pocket, buzzes during a bedtime story, and lies awake in the dark. A workday with no ending doesn't stay where it was put.

It leaks into everything else: the meal, the friend, the sleep. The opening pages of the Bible tell a story of work with its ending built in, and other traditions draw the line in their own ways. Today: Compline.

teach.h: IT WAS VERY GOOD. GOD ENDED.
teach.b: First, Genesis. At the end of the sixth day, the King James Bible says, "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." Then: "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made."
Look at it, call it good, end it. In this story the ending isn't an interruption of the making. It's part of it.

Its ninth chapter warns against filling a vessel to the brim and carrying it full, and against sharpening a blade so keen it can't keep its edge. When the work is done, it says, withdrawing is the way of Heaven.
Not hanging on. Not one more email. Third, the monastery.
The Rule of Benedict closes the monks' day with the night prayer called Compline, and after it, the Rule says, no one may speak. The day's work, and even the day's talk, gets a clear edge.
Fourth, an ending for an ordinary job. It can be small.

teach.h: LOOK BACK, WRITE IT DOWN, CLOSE.
teach.b: Look back at what got done, the way Genesis looks back, and let some of it be good.

Write down what's left, so the mind can set it down. Then mark the line: a phrase, a closed door, a walk, a change of clothes. A clear end protects the rest of life: the people at home, the friends, the sleep.
It also protects the work, which comes back the next morning to someone rested.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns end the day with Compline and keep silence afterward; Jews and Christians read the close of the creation story in Genesis as a pattern of work that ends; readers of the Tao Te Ching return to its ninth chapter on stepping back when the work is done.

games.q: a long project has gone well, and your name is starting to be known for it. what does chapter nine of the Tao Te Ching say to do?
o: keep pushing while your name is rising.
withdraw, for that is the way of Heaven.
games.why: when the work is done, it says, withdrawing is the way of Heaven. a full vessel and an over-sharpened blade are its pictures of not stopping.

practice: Name one thing from today's work, or yesterday's, that got done, however small, and look at it for a moment, the way Genesis looks back.
Then name one thing left undone, picture writing it down for tomorrow, and say silently: done for today. Let the shoulders drop; if you pray, you can close the work in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Compline. The monks' night prayer in the Rule of Benedict, after which no one may speak, giving the day a clear edge. Today's word.
